milestone: The dashboard stopped crying wolf about a perfectly healthy Kafka
description: The system-health panel had been flashing one of Alfr3d's core services as CRITICAL, at zero percent health, roughly one refresh in seven -- while the service was in perfect shape the whole time. Two things were wrong. The panel read processor load in a unit that could exceed its own maximum on a multi-core machine, so a brief spike wrapped around into an alarm. More fundamentally, it was treating "working hard" as "about to die", which is exactly backwards for a service whose job is to handle bursts. Health now comes from each container's own self-test rather than being inferred from how busy it looks, so a component can be under load and still read as green, and a bar that fills up means work getting done rather than something going wrong. Along the way, every container that had no self-test got one -- thirteen of thirteen now report a real verdict, where only five did before -- and three services that had quietly dropped off the panel entirely, invisible for ten days, are back on it.

milestone: The dashboard's loading spinners became something with a personality
description: Every generic loading spinner and plain circular button outline across the web dashboard and the Deck launcher's radial menu was replaced with the same family of animated rings -- three shapes that mean something specific (acquiring a lock, syncing with the backend, working something out) and five more that just tell menu items apart. The rings never sit perfectly still, and only really freeze when something's actually wrong, so a resting screen still reads as alive rather than idle. People who prefer reduced motion get the same information through colour alone, with the spinning turned off. The design is a from-scratch recreation of a set of animated HUD buttons by designer Goran Spasojevic, credited in both apps.

milestone: Alfr3d notices when a guest has quietly become part of the household
description: Alfr3d used to treat every guest the same, whether they'd dropped by for an hour or been staying for weeks -- the same headcount card, the same flat lift to the house's music energy, day after day. It now tracks how long a guest has been continuously staying, and that influence fades the longer they're around: a brand-new guest still lifts the mood the way it always has, but a guest who's clearly settled in stops reading as a party starting, and can even nudge things back toward an ordinary quiet day. Past about two weeks of an unbroken stay, Alfr3d suggests actually addressing it -- promoting them to a resident, or having the conversation -- rather than quietly letting it drift. Deployed to the house the same day, right after a full database backup.

milestone: Alfr3d can now tell you when a room feels off
description: The temperature and humidity readings from that first real ESPHome sensor now do something: if a room gets too warm, too cold, too humid, or too dry, Alfr3d says so on the dashboard. It only speaks up when the sensor's connection is actually current, so a stale reading from a flaky Wi-Fi link can't trigger a false alert.

milestone: Alfr3d learned what's normal for your house, hour by hour
description: The comfort alerts above used fixed, one-size-fits-all thresholds because Alfr3d had never kept a history of what a room's temperature and humidity actually look like at different times of day. It does now -- every reading from a real sensor is recorded, and a new alert compares the current reading against what's typical for that specific hour, not a flat number. A cool morning no longer looks the same as a cool afternoon. Deployed to the house the same day, right after a full database backup; the fixed-threshold alert fired live within minutes of the update, and the new history started filling in immediately. This more precise alert will stay quiet for a while until enough history builds up to trust it.

milestone: A leftover integration was quietly broadcasting household activity -- removed
description: An old integration had kept forwarding a copy of the household's live activity feed to a public notification service, unauthenticated -- anyone who found the right address could have watched it happen in real time. It was dead code left over from a phone-notification experiment the household stopped using years ago. Found and removed the same day it was noticed.

milestone: Alfr3d's ESPHome support met its first real sensor
description: ESPHome -- the open, cloud-free firmware many cheap smart sensors run -- has been supported since August, but never actually tested against a real device. The first one to join a real household, a temperature and humidity sensor, immediately surfaced a real bug: the scan that finds ESPHome devices on the network was running from the wrong place internally, and would have silently found nothing on any real home network. Fixed, and a way to add a device by its network address directly was added for networks where the automatic scan still can't reach it. Live temperature, humidity, and signal readings are now flowing from a real sensor in a real house for the first time. Shipped in v0.4.4.

milestone: A live sensor reading could have crashed its own display -- fixed first
description: Found while getting that first real ESPHome sensor onto the dashboard: opening its control panel to see the live reading would have crashed the panel outright, because the sensor's data was stored in a shape the display code didn't expect. Caught and fixed in the same session, before any real user ran into it.

milestone: Alfr3d's memory of the household now spans two years
description: Alfr3d used to forget most of what it noticed about the household after 90 to 180 days -- not long enough to compare this winter to last summer, when routines shift with daylight and school schedules. Its situational-awareness history (arrivals and departures, attention patterns, app interactions, device locations) now keeps two full years, with disk growth tracked over time so that horizon keeps being trustworthy.

milestone: Alfr3d's brain and its launcher stopped guessing separately
description: Alfr3d's brain and Alfr3d Deck each used to guess the time of day, whether you were busy, and what your phone was doing -- separately, and the guesses didn't always agree. A wind-down suggestion firing at the wrong hour on a real Saturday evening exposed just how far apart they could get: over three hours, in one real case. Now each fact is owned by whichever side actually knows it -- the brain is the source of truth for time-of-day and routines, the Deck is the source of truth for its own battery, do-not-disturb, and connection state -- and the two share what they know instead of re-deriving it independently. If one side can't be reached, the other falls back to its own best estimate rather than showing nothing. Deployed to the house and confirmed working the same day.

milestone: The launcher has a new name: Alfr3d Deck
description: "Nexus" now belongs to the web dashboard alone, so the launcher dropped the name it used to share with it -- it's Alfr3d Deck now, its radial thumb-menu is Socket, and its terminal is Alfr3d Shell.
First-launch setup was rebuilt: a five-step walkthrough for permissions, connecting to the house, and setting Alfr3d Deck as your home screen, verified end to end on a real phone.
Long-press any app, anywhere in the launcher, for a real context menu -- app info and uninstall -- instead of nothing happening.
The app list now survives being killed by the system in the background, so opening the app drawer after a cold start no longer means waiting through a fresh scan.

Found and fixed a real crash: reinstalling the launcher, or restoring it onto a new phone, could crash on every launch afterward because Android's backup system was restoring encrypted sign-in data whose key doesn't survive a reinstall. It now recovers on its own instead of getting stuck.
Moved to a newer Android build toolchain to stay ahead of Google's requirements.

milestone: Alfr3d learns your comings and goings -- with your consent
description: With your explicit, opt-in consent, Alfr3d can learn your movements away from home -- not just whether you are on the house Wi-Fi -- so it comes to understand your daily rhythm well enough to anticipate when you are heading out or have the house ready for your return. It is off by default and stays that way until you deliberately turn it on. The location is approximate, never precise tracking; it goes only to your own Alfr3d server and is never sent to Littl3.1 Engineering or anyone else; the launcher reads it only while you are using your phone, never in the background; and switching it off stops collection and clears anything still queued. Shipped, deployed, and live-verified against real production data -- released as Alfr3d Deck v0.2.2.

milestone: The "leave by now" card is live in a real house
description: The leave-by travel card fired for the first time in an actual household: a real calendar event with an address, a real drive time computed on the self-hosted routing engine, a real "leave by 10:18 AM" on the dashboard -- no staging, no mock-up. Two fixes got it there. Alfr3d now re-checks the calendar every fifteen minutes on its own, so an event you just added shows up without waiting for a restart. And event times now read in the household's own timezone instead of UTC -- a 5pm event created in a European calendar had been showing as 3pm on a North American screen. Deployed to the house the same day.

milestone: littl31.com leads with the butler, not the category
description: The site now leads with what Alfr3d is -- "the only home butler you own" -- instead of a category label that read like a lesser Home Assistant, and that shift carries into the page titles and a new "Getting Alfr3d" section on the home page that points to the full lineup and pricing. Every feature claim on the product page was checked against what the situational-awareness engine actually does in production: the "leave by now" example was reworded so it no longer implies live-traffic knowledge it doesn't have, and a line that implied every feature is already running was softened, since the self-hosted routing behind the leave-by card still has to be switched on per household. The home page also carries a dormant slot for a short screen recording of that leave-by card in action, to drop in once it's captured.

milestone: Deck keeps up with the house in the background
description: Until now the launcher only talked to Alfr3d while one of its windows was open and the screen was on. It now checks in roughly every half hour on its own -- only on a charged-enough battery, backing off politely when the network is bad -- so weather, who's home, and the situational-awareness cards are already current the moment you pick the device up. When a genuinely new card appears while the screen is off (say, "the garage light is still on"), it raises exactly one quiet notification that the next card replaces rather than stacks. There's a Background Sync card in Settings to turn it off or sync on demand. Verified on a real device against the live house system, including two bugs found and fixed in the process.

milestone: Pricing rounded to whole numbers -- every ".99" ending dropped
description: Every ".99"-ending price across the live lineup was rounded to a whole number -- the site's honesty-first positioning (bragging about what got killed in honesty.html) sat oddly next to $X.99 psychology pricing. Deck Pro unlock $5.99 -> $6 one-time; Kit Founding-100 $399 -> $400; Kit Steady-state $449 -> $450; Uplink $9.99/mo -> $10/mo and $99/yr -> $100/yr. Shipped the same day as real CAD/USD/EUR currency-rotation on the pricing switcher.

milestone: Deck radial menu tidied up
description: The spatial launcher's radial menu was reorganised so the common destinations sit one level shallower: the terminal moved in with the apps, and Settings and Search now sit directly under System next to Power instead of behind an extra submenu. The top ring stays four choices and nothing is more than three steps deep. The in-app About text was also rewritten in a rougher, more first-person voice.

milestone: Alfr3d can be told what to call you
description: Alfr3d's language model was never told who it was speaking to, so its more formal moods fell back on a generic, gendered "sir or madam". Each resident can now set a preferred form of address -- a first name, "boss", "Dr. Athos", whatever -- from the web UI or the launcher's Residents editor. The voice uses it occasionally rather than every line, falls back to the username if it's unset, and "sir"/"madam" are now banned outright. The field is stored per person so it's ready when Alfr3d can tell residents apart by voice.

milestone: NEXUS SHELL: a real terminal inside the launcher
description: The launcher's terminal grew from a toy into a genuine command line, shipped in five phases and verified on a real device at each step.
It can manage the device: list, launch and inspect installed apps, and read device and settings state.
It has a working filesystem CLI for moving around and inspecting files.

It reaches into Alfr3d itself: control devices, tail the live event stream, and read the current context and mood card (falling back to a local estimate, honestly labelled, when Alfr3d's own mood card isn't present).

It can drive the launcher's own window manager -- list, focus and close windows, and save or restore named layouts (Pro-gated to match the existing layout-presets feature). Building this surfaced and fixed a real latent bug in closing a minimised window.

milestone: Alfr3d learned to tell time
description: Alfr3d greeted the house with "Good morning!" at 10pm. Six different parts of the system each did their own time-of-day math and disagreed, and the voice had no clock at all. They now share one source of truth, built from the household's own wake / sleep / sunrise / sunset routines: it decides when Alfr3d is awake enough to speak, tells the language model what time it actually is (so it won't wish you good morning at night), leads a welcome-home with the right greeting, and lets the small talk wind down in the last stretch before bed. Deployed and verified on the real house system.

milestone: Deck pre-launch polish + rebrand (v0.1.35)
description: The launcher was renamed from "Spatial Launcher" to "Alfr3d Nexus Launcher" in the in-app About/header copy, tagged v0.1.35 -- it became Alfr3d Deck in the later Sep 2026 rename.

A pre-submission pass cleared the Play Store technical and policy hygiene: targeting Android 16 (API 36) to meet Google's first-submission requirement, code shrinking and resource minification turned on for release builds and verified on a real device, and a privacy-policy gap closed (an every-15-minute attention-telemetry report to the backend that wasn't disclosed).
Store listing, screenshots, and release notes were rewritten to match everything shipped since the first draft.

Devices window gained the ability to delete a device (tap-to-arm confirm), plus fixes for a chip-row that wrapped instead of scrolling and a connection check that showed a false "connected" state on an http-to-https redirect.
What's left before it goes live is account-holder-only Play Console setup.

milestone: Voice restraint + two more UI themes
description: Alfr3d's personality quirks -- the little verbal tics and swapped-in quips -- were firing on every single thing it said, which made the bit wear thin fast. They're now occasional, roughly one utterance in eight, on both the language-model path and the no-model fallback path.
Two more dashboard themes shipped alongside the existing three: Matrix (green terminal) and Steel/Graphite.

milestone: Backend: August 2026 in review
description: Full JWT Auth + RBAC shipped across all 5 phases: backend login/refresh/logout, a permission matrix on all 56 write routes, webapp + Deck sign-in, rate limiting, no username enumeration, self-service/admin password reset -- tagged v0.2.0.
Every integration credential (Home Assistant, SmartThings, Spotify, ESPHome) is now Fernet-encrypted at rest, with a zero-downtime dual-read fallback for existing plaintext rows.
ESPHome added as a new local-only IoT provider, alongside a device-registry-backed multi-camera streaming model.
Household user management landed end to end: self-service profile editing, full owner/admin CRUD and password-reset, and first-run onboarding for new installs.

A durable household event log replaced a 20-item RAM buffer; a card feedback loop lets situational-awareness cards learn when a household ignores them; a shared per-cycle context frame cut redundant DB reads by about a third.
Learned baselines widened from single appliances to per-resident departure times and a household-level "is today unusual" check.

A 12-item situational-awareness roadmap deployed to production in one pass -- event log, card feedback, calendar conferencing, structured cards, anomaly detection, self-hosted routing, plus 3 items investigated and correctly stopped on real evidence.
Leave-by travel guidance rebuilt on a self-hosted OSRM routing engine plus the free Nominatim geocoding API -- no Google API key, no per-trip cloud call.
A Nexus quick-controls panel shipped: up to 10 favorited smarthome devices as toggle/dial tiles, opened from the Nexus Core.
Repos migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org, and the Kit's hardware base switched from a Raspberry Pi 5 to an N100 mini PC, restoring margin after a CAD-verified cost check.

milestone: Deck: August 2026 in review
description: Free spatial launcher with a $5.99 one-time Pro unlock live since v0.1.28 -- CI builds a debug APK on every push, with a signed-release workflow on version tags.
Custom Colors theming shipped as a 5th Pro feature: user-defined accent colors via an in-app HSV picker.
Added a rotation-lock setting and required sign-in (Keystore-backed credentials) for write actions -- device control, resident edits, running or editing a routine.
Gained the leave-by travel-guidance display, backed by the new self-hosted routing engine.
Repo migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org.

milestone: Situational awareness cards: August 2026 in review
description: Household composition awareness: a card reading who's home versus away, and known versus unknown devices, surfaced on the Ambient Brief with urgency-aware styling.

Cross-surface continuity: a new backend endpoint plus routines and now-playing tracking, so the launcher can offer to pick up where you left off -- resuming music paused elsewhere, or a routine edited on the web dashboard.
Rhythm-break anomalies: learns each device's typical on/off rhythm from history and flags anything still on well past its usual pattern, such as a light left on much later than normal.
Attention telemetry: the launcher reports rolling attention and dwell telemetry to a new backend endpoint, feeding the focus and wind-down signals.
All four were built and unit-tested on both sides, but none was verified on-device, and the rhythm-break baselines had no real data accumulated yet.

milestone: littl31.com: August 2026 in review
description: Site launched at littl31.com: index.html (pitch), alfr3d.html (product + pricing), lab.html (R&D showcase).

alfr3d.html got real descriptive copy for the Launcher, Core, Cloud, and Kit cards, plus a fix for a scroll-reveal crash that had been silently blocking content sitewide; a splash-logo animation crash on the homepage was also fixed.

Pricing strategy evolved across the month: from the original Core/Launcher/Cloud plan, to a Kit-first ladder ($399 Founding-100 / $449 steady-state plus a Butler subscription), to a simplified 3-SKU lineup -- then a CAD-verified parts-cost check found the Kit underwater on margin, prompting a hardware pivot from a Raspberry Pi 5 to a cheaper N100 mini PC.
Repos migrated to the Littl3-1-Engineering GitHub org.

milestone: Alfr3d Uplink: August 2026 in review
description: Pricing strategy evolved across the month: Cloud and Cloud+ were retired as tier names, folded into a new Relay + Butler ladder, then simplified further by folding Relay into Butler. A CAD-verified cost check on the Kit (which bundles free Relay for life) prompted a hardware pivot from a Raspberry Pi 5 to a cheaper N100 mini PC to protect margin.

milestone: Alfred Cube
description: Earliest known concept/build in the Alfr3d lineage.

milestone: MK-I
description: Early 2014 iteration of the home-automation daemon.

milestone: MK-III
description: 2014 iteration, ordering relative to MK-I/MK-II unconfirmed.

milestone: MK-II
description: Home-automation daemon running on a Pi (/home/alfr3d/alfr3ddaemon.py), audio handling.
Added Python LIFX integration (pylifx).

milestone: Split into dedicated repos
description: Server + mobile companion apps split out: Alfr3dServer, Alfr3d4Android-Original, Alfr3d-MKIII-Android, alfr3d.io.

milestone: Alfr3d-MKIV (new architecture)
description: Separate repo from the 2015 MK-IV Notion page, not yet reconciled with it.

milestone: Bedouina ("Bena")
description: Repo explicitly describes itself as "Successor to Project Alfr3d" -- a rebrand attempt that didn't end up replacing it. Active Feb 2018 to Oct 2020 (239 commits, confirmed via GitHub commit history).

milestone: Cassiop3ia / MK-VI
description: First Kafka message-bus architecture (topics speak/environment/device/user) -- direct architectural precursor to today's Kafka-based backend. Active Sep 2022 through May 2026 (434 commits) -- notably overlapping with the start of the current consolidated rewrite rather than a clean handoff.

milestone: Alfr3d Kit build + BOM validation
description: Build one Kit end-to-end and time assembly before publishing the $400 Founding-100 price. Validates the current ~$235 CAD parts-cost estimate (N100 mini PC, NVMe SSD, PSU, enclosure, cooling, cabling, packaging) plus assembly labor, shipping, fees, and a support/DOA reserve against a real build, not just parts pricing.

milestone: littl31.com commerce: Stripe Checkout + Founding 100 preorder
description: Top GTM priority: give the Kit and Cloud pricing tiers a real visitor-to-customer path -- every rendered CTA is still a mailto: waitlist link. Backend checkout wiring staged 2026-09-09: create-checkout-session now sells only catalogued products (kit-founding, kit-steady, uplink-annual, uplink-monthly) through a server-side product-key -> STRIPE_PRICE_* map in functions/_shared/catalog.js, never a caller-supplied price ID, so test-to-live is an env-var change. Each of those four tiers in content.yml carries a dormant checkout block that no template reads yet. Still gated, nothing charges a card: no Stripe Prices or secrets set, no checkout frontend, no subscriber storage (webhook.js cases remain stubs pending the Cloud relay identity store). Remaining: create the Stripe Prices (multi-currency), set the Pages secrets, build the checkout frontend + success/cancel states, wire the webhook to subscriber storage, update pricing copy + privacy policy section 2.

milestone: Repo tooling standardization (all 3 repos)
description: alfr3d_deck brought up to alfr3d's baseline: pre-commit-hooks (trailing-whitespace/end-of-file/yaml/large-files) + detect-secrets (fresh baseline, one expected finding -- keystore.properties.sample's changeme placeholders), Dependabot for gradle + github-actions. alfr3d_deck already had CI (build.yml, release.yml) -- ahead of alfr3d there, whose own ci.yml is actually .disabled (a stale claim in this todo corrected). littl31 and Aikido (needs external account signup) still open.

milestone: SmartThings generic IoT control endpoint — fixed, pending live-device verification
description: Fixed 2026-08-24, same day it was found: control_iot_device() (routes/iot.py) now has a source=='smartthings' branch using a new st_utils.translate_generic_control_params() that mirrors the HA translator, mapping ControlBlade's generic command vocabulary to an ST (capability, command, args) triple. sync_st_devices() now also derives device_type via a new st_utils.normalize_st_device_type() from the device's capability list, instead of storing ST's raw deviceTypeName label -- confirmed nothing else in the codebase read that raw label. Both pieces are code-complete and committed; still needs verification against a live SmartThings device, which is the only reason this isn't Shipped yet.

milestone: Per-token LLM usage display
description: Personality panel currently shows call-count usage only; per-token usage metadata from the LLM client isn't surfaced yet. Minor — a future-enhancement aside, not a scoped plan.

milestone: Alfr3d Deck Cloud pairing
description: Push notifications to the launcher; depends on Alfr3d Cloud Phase 3 shipping first.

milestone: Spotify now-playing via launcher push
description: Have the launcher push on-device now-playing (any media session, not just Spotify) to the backend instead of only backend-side polling. Documented as a deferred fast-follow, not yet scoped.

milestone: littl31.com roadmap
description: Its own todo/ folder was checked directly and contains only a completed bugfix note (mobile scramble jitter fix); no forward-looking roadmap items exist for the site itself.

milestone: Multi-source audio (beyond Spotify)
description: Abstract audio-source interface so playback isn't Spotify-only — local library, Tidal, YouTube Music, radio — plus a loose future-ideas list (NLU voice control, Last.fm scrobbling, multi-room sync).

milestone: Alfr3d Deck Play Store publishing
description: Signing, Gradle Play Publisher, and gated CI already wired up; blocked on manual account-holder steps: Play developer enrollment, Play Console app entry, first manual release upload, sensitive-permission declarations + demo video, hosted privacy policy URL, CI service account for future automated releases.

milestone: Multi-user calendar/email attribution
description: Attribute calendar/Gmail integrations to individual household members instead of one shared global account. Blocked on Auth + RBAC landing first.

milestone: Camera streaming roadmap (WebRTC / recording / CV)
description: Three parked options beyond the already-shipped HLS pipeline: WebRTC for sub-500ms latency, recorded/archived playback, and computer-vision motion/person detection.

milestone: Alfr3d Cloud (Phase 3)
description: Remote-access relay (no port forwarding) + push notifications; "thin, dumb-pipe relay" that never sees plaintext data. Now scoped into a phased plan in todo_cloud_relay.md: architecture spike -> subscriber/billing identity + Stripe -> relay/tunnel -> FCM push -> security review. Deliberately a separate identity system from household RBAC auth. Not yet built.

milestone: Hardware enclosure design
description: Physical enclosure for the ALFR3D device + peripherals (mic/speaker/camera/sensors), matching the dark tactical/glassmorphic visual identity. Not currently scheduled — blocked on the hardware phase starting and a finalized bill of materials.

milestone: Kit ordering / Cloud signup commerce plan
description: Phased plan to give the Kit and Cloud pricing sections a real path from visitor to paying customer — site currently has zero CTA/checkout links on either tier. Phase A: free waitlist/interest-capture forms. Phase B (gated on Kit waitlist signal): Stripe Checkout for the one-time Kit purchase. Phase C (gated on the Cloud relay being built): Stripe Checkout + Customer Portal + magic-link login alongside the relay's own subscriber identity. Planning only, not started.

milestone: Self-awareness: pronounce own name + don't self-greet
description: Both identity bugs fixed 2026-08-27, not yet on-device verified: normalize_pronunciation() in service_speak regex-substitutes the leetspeak "alfr3d" to "Alfred" right before every TTS call, and update_user_state() in service_user now guards the welcome-greeting flow so the alfr3d system user never announces itself coming online like a household member (its presence-state row still updates normally). A closer look also found the guard is currently dead/defensive code -- no code path in the schema seed or the three runtime user-insert sites ever creates a row with username='alfr3d'.

milestone: CAD BOM correction + revised CAGR/monetization strategy
description: Recommended-tier Kit parts corrected from $191 (a USD-MSRP artifact) to ~$425 CAD verified Canadian pricing -- Founding-100 ($399) now underwater on parts alone before the N100 pivot above. Added a market CAGR range (12-20% working estimate) and a revised pricing/sales plan: budget-tier storage default, Founding-100 reframed as a small hand-assembled batch, Butler subscription as the primary margin engine. Realistic Year 1: 40-100 Kit units; Year 2: 150-400 cumulative.

milestone: Explore: Alfr3d Deck as a new context source for situational awareness
description: Explore feeding the launcher's own on-device signals (attention/dwell, foreground app, etc.) back into the backend's situational-awareness engine as a new context source, alongside existing presence/device signals. One candidate signal, BLE presence sensing, was investigated directly and set aside (see "BLE presence sensing -- explored and set aside" above) -- modern phones rotate their Bluetooth address, so nothing personally-carried stayed identifiable in a real scan. The rest of the signal list (WiFi leave/arrive, named context zones, car Bluetooth, etc.) remains unexplored.

milestone: Clean up GitHub CI/CD, security & Aikido CVEs (all repos)
description: CI/CD + security cleanup across all three repos: re-enable alfr3d's disabled ci.yml, finish Aikido signup for littl31, and triage/remediate CVEs Aikido flags once scanning is live across alfr3d, alfr3d_deck, and Littl31. Distinct from Repo tooling standardization (pre-commit/detect-secrets/Dependabot baseline) -- this is the CI pipeline health + vulnerability remediation pass. Not started.

milestone: BLE presence sensing -- explored and set aside
description: The household's hardware can scan for BLE devices just fine, but real scans found no personal device (phone, watch) with a stable enough identity to track -- modern phones deliberately rotate their Bluetooth address. Only fixed smart-home gear (TVs, a smart light) stayed identifiable, which isn't useful as a presence signal. Re-checked again a few weeks later, just in case -- same result, same devices, same verdict. Set aside unless a wearable with a genuinely stable address enters the household.

milestone: "What usually happens next" pattern learning
description: A planned next step for the household event log -- noticing that one event usually follows another, and gently flagging it when it doesn't -- needs real weeks of history to learn from honestly. The event log itself is brand new, so this is queued rather than built against too little data.

milestone: Locking down the site with a Content-Security-Policy header
description: A routine security scan flagged that the site doesn't set a Content-Security-Policy header -- the standard first line of defense against a compromised script running attacker code in a visitor's browser. The site is static and hosted on GitHub Pages, which doesn't support custom response headers, so this needs a fix at the Cloudflare layer in front of it rather than a code change. Not started yet.
